explanations.answer: Take your positions and prepare yourself
explanations.explanation: That's the call: “Take your positions and prepare yourself, for the sword devours those around you.” (Jeremiah 46:14) It's a get-ready message, and it goes out loud to Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes. So the answer is about getting into position, not sitting still.

explanations.answer: Open your gates and welcome the king
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The message doesn't say a word about gates or welcoming anybody. It says to take your positions and prepare yourself, because the sword devours those around you.

explanations.answer: Lay down your weapons and rest awhile
explanations.explanation: I like the relaxed energy, but the verse goes the other direction. It says to take your positions and prepare yourself, because the sword devours those around you. Nothing in it says to lay down weapons or rest.

Yes, the LORD. The text says the warriors cannot stand, “…for the LORD has thrust them down.” (Jeremiah 46:15) So this isn't a clumsy day or a slippery floor. It's the LORD's doing, and that changes how you read the whole scene.

Pharaoh is the king of Egypt in this passage, so I see why he came to mind. But the text says it's the LORD who has thrust the warriors down. Pharaoh gets his own mention a few verses later, and it isn't a flattering one.
No priest shows up in this verse, friend. The one doing the thrusting is the LORD. Sometimes the answer is the same name that opened the whole message.

True! The warriors say, “Get up! Let us return to our people and to the land of our birth, away from the sword of the oppressor.” (Jeremiah 46:16) That's a whole group saying they want out of there. So going back to their own people and the land of their birth is exactly what the text has them say.

It's actually true, friend. The warriors say, “Get up! Let us return to our people and to the land of our birth, away from the sword of the oppressor.” (Jeremiah 46:16) So going back to their own people and birthplace is exactly what they say. They want away from the sword.

explanations.answer: He was all noise and let his time pass
explanations.explanation: Right on. They cry out, “Pharaoh king of Egypt was all noise; he has let the appointed time pass him by.” (Jeremiah 46:17) That's a lot of volume and not much follow-through. I know that feeling. I once stamped a whole tray of cookies and forgot to turn the oven on.

explanations.answer: He fought for them to the very end
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what they say. The cry is that Pharaoh was all noise and let the appointed time pass him by. Nothing in the verse says he fought for them. Big talk, then a missed moment.

explanations.answer: He sent them help right on time
explanations.explanation: Close to the opposite, friend. The verse says he has let the appointed time pass him by. So the timing was missed, and the help never shows up in the words they cry out. All they have to say about him is that he was all noise.
True. The King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts, says, “As surely as I live…” (Jeremiah 46:18) That's a promise sworn on His own life. When He says one is coming, you can count on it.

It's actually true, friend. The LORD begins with “As surely as I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts…” (Jeremiah 46:18) That's an oath on His own life. So what He says next stands on the strongest ground there is.

Exile it is. The LORD says, “Pack your bags for exile, O daughter dwelling in Egypt!” (Jeremiah 46:19) Memphis will be laid waste, destroyed and uninhabited, so staying put isn't the plan. It's a heavy line.
Battle sounds reasonable, but that's not the word the LORD uses. The verse says, “Pack your bags for exile, O daughter dwelling in Egypt!” It also says Memphis will be laid waste and uninhabited.
Nice thought, but the verse doesn't send her to worship. It says, “Pack your bags for exile, O daughter dwelling in Egypt!” Memphis is about to be laid waste, destroyed and uninhabited.

A gadfly! The LORD says, “Egypt is a beautiful heifer, but a gadfly from the north is coming against her.” (Jeremiah 46:20) A gadfly is a pesky fly, and the picture is a beautiful animal being pestered by something small. Anybody who's tried to swat one knows it's no small trouble.

A lion would make for a dramatic picture, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says a gadfly from the north is coming against the heifer. A fly is a different kind of problem, the kind that circles and circles.
Big guess, but no bear in this verse. The LORD says a gadfly from the north is coming against the beautiful heifer. It's a smaller animal than you were picturing, friend, and a way more annoying one.

That one is false, friend. The verse says the mercenaries “…will turn back; together they will flee, they will not stand their ground…” (Jeremiah 46:21) So standing their ground is exactly what they won't do. The day of calamity is coming upon them.

False is right. The text says the mercenaries “…will turn back; together they will flee, they will not stand their ground, for the day of calamity is coming upon them…” (Jeremiah 46:21) They're called like fattened calves, and no one is holding the line. Everybody heads for the exit together.

A serpent! The text says, “Egypt will hiss like a fleeing serpent, for the enemy will advance in force…” (Jeremiah 46:22) That's the sound of something slithering off in a hurry. The enemy advancing in force is what sets it off.

A deer is a fair guess for a fleeing animal, but this verse picks something that hisses. The text says Egypt will hiss like a fleeing serpent. A deer hissing would be a confusing afternoon for everybody.
Horses can run, friend, but they don't hiss. The text says Egypt will hiss like a fleeing serpent as the enemy advances in force. If a horse hissed at me, I'd lose my hat.

explanations.answer: They are more numerous than locusts
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The LORD says they will chop down her forest, “…dense though it may be, for they are more numerous than locusts; they cannot be counted.” (Jeremiah 46:23) So it isn't about the trees being weak. It's about how many are coming.

explanations.answer: They set the whole forest on fire
explanations.explanation: Fire is a creative guess, but the verse never mentions it. The enemy comes with axes, like woodsmen cutting down trees. They chop the forest down because they are more numerous than locusts. It's all axes and numbers.

explanations.answer: The trees have already dried out
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about dry trees. It says the forest is dense, and the enemy chops it down anyway, because they are more numerous than locusts. They cannot be counted. So the reason is the size of the army, not the condition of the trees.

True. The text says, “The Daughter of Egypt will be put to shame; she will be delivered into the hands of the people of the north.” (Jeremiah 46:24) Both things are said together in that one verse. It's a heavy line.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says, “The Daughter of Egypt will be put to shame; she will be delivered into the hands of the people of the north.” (Jeremiah 46:24) Shame and being handed over are in the same breath. It's a heavy line.

Thebes is right. The LORD says, “Behold, I am about to punish Amon god of Thebes, along with Pharaoh, Egypt with her gods and kings, and those who trust in Pharaoh.” (Jeremiah 46:25) So Amon is named right there with Egypt's gods. It's a long list, and you kept up.

Zoan isn't the name this verse gives. The LORD says He is about to punish “…Amon god of Thebes…” (Jeremiah 46:25) It's a lot of names to juggle, friend, and I've dropped a whole tray of cookies over less.
On is a short name, which makes it easy to grab. But the verse says, “…Amon god of Thebes…” (Jeremiah 46:25) Thebes is the one the text gives. Next time, check the long name first.

explanations.answer: It will be inhabited as in days of old
explanations.explanation: Yes! The LORD says, “But after this, Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 46:26) After the hard part, people live there again. That little word “after” does a lot of work in this verse.

explanations.answer: It will stay empty for all time
explanations.explanation: I get it, with all that destruction talk. But the LORD says, “But after this, Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old…” (Jeremiah 46:26) So empty isn't the last word. People will live there again.

explanations.answer: It will be covered over by the sea
explanations.explanation: No sea in this verse, friend. The LORD says that after this, Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old. So the story for Egypt doesn't end with the hard part. It turns toward people living there again.

That's the word to Jacob. The LORD says, “But you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid, and do not be dismayed, O Israel.” (Jeremiah 46:27) After all that noise about Egypt, here comes a gentle turn. The text puts Jacob and Israel side by side.

The verse doesn't tell him to stay put. The LORD tells Jacob, “…do not be afraid, and do not be dismayed…” (Jeremiah 46:27) He also says He will save Jacob out of a distant place. That's a long way from staying where you are.

Hills sound like a smart hiding spot, but the LORD doesn't send Jacob there. He says, “…do not be afraid, and do not be dismayed, O Israel.” (Jeremiah 46:27) He also says He will save Jacob out of a distant place.

Ease! The text says, “Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid.” (Jeremiah 46:27) Quiet and ease, and nobody around to scare him. That sounds like the best porch in the world.
Toil is hard work, and I love hard work, but that's not the word here. The verse says Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid. It's a peaceful picture, not a grind.

I see why that came to mind after a heavy passage. But the verse promises, “Jacob will return to quiet and ease, with no one to make him afraid.” (Jeremiah 46:27) Ease is the word for where this part ends up.
That's the reason. The LORD says, “And you, My servant Jacob, do not be afraid, declares the LORD, for I am with you.” (Jeremiah 46:28) It isn't a plan or a map. The reason is that He is with Jacob.

Egypt is the one facing punishment in this passage, friend, so that's not where the comfort comes from. The reason the LORD gives is, “…for I am with you.” (Jeremiah 46:28) His presence is the whole reason.
Nothing in the verse says that. The LORD's reason is, “…for I am with you.” (Jeremiah 46:28) Distance doesn't come into it. It's His presence that Jacob gets to lean on.

That one is false, friend. The LORD says, “Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished.” (Jeremiah 46:28) So there is discipline. It comes right alongside the promise that He won't completely destroy Jacob.

False is right. The LORD says, “Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished.” (Jeremiah 46:28) He won't completely destroy Jacob, and He also won't skip the discipline. Both are in the same verse, and I think that's worth sitting with.
